videos.script: A release that goes wrong needs two decisions. When to stop it, and how to go back. {{two}} This lesson makes the first one before the release starts. Four numbers at the top of a script say how much worse is too much, and how much evidence is enough. {{criteria}} Then the script runs a canary with nobody watching. It stops the release with the bug at the second step, and sends every customer back. {{abort}} It also has a flaw, and you will see it. Between fifty and ninety-nine answers, one unlucky error is enough to stop a good release. {{flaw}} Then rollback, on an environment with no router. Under two seconds, because the old release never left the disk. And two surprises worth meeting on a calm day: a second rollback goes forward again, and a first deploy has nothing to go back to. {{rollback}} After that, what a rollback cannot undo: a migration, an e-mail, a payment. {{data}} The lesson ends where every incident should. A test that fails on the old code and passes on the fix, a short postmortem with no culprit in it, and a budget that says when to stop releasing altogether. {{end}}
